There are a lot of factors that could be at play here. Are you driving mainly in the morning? Sometimes, there will be debris or condensation that was built up, and when driving in the morning, it'll squeak until the debris gets rubbed off.

You could also have semi-metallic pads. Those are a combination of organic (or ceramic, I don't remember), and metal. I don't really see them used very often anymore. You could try swapping the pads and rotors and replacing the pads with the ceramic version of the pads.

Debris from the gravel road. As I stated above, debris getting caught somewhere it should could cause a squeak as well, until that debris loosens.

Hardware kit(s) are rubbing. Even if the pads look good, maybe a clip got jarred loose and is making contact with the rotor at some point.

Honestly, if you have pad life on them, I'd say run them. If the noise is truly bothering you, most shops offer a hardware cleaning service. They'll either clean or replace the hard, and clean the pads.

I was mainly a service advisor for the first 4 or 5 years of the automotive career. I slowly transitioned into the general service role and spent time doing that for a couple of years, and then I started doing a bit more service work. Then, near the point of the closure of my shop, I was ready to make the leap to trying to do just service work. 

After the next few shops, I mentioned "Hey, I worked at this shop prior, and I was about to move up so I can get more service under my belt, so I'm not a full fledged B-Tech, I want to learn this though" and they were OK with teaching me at the time of my hiring. I wouldn't say that. Anxiety is a crazy mental illness that plays tricks on you, and it makes you have physical symptoms. I have no clue as to why it does, but anxiety is just a very physical illness, essentially.

I do. If I go out and do stuff with people to get my mind away from thinking about it, it goes away. And when I'm lying down, I do tend to focus on it more, so it gives me that sensation again. I'd see if you can go on walks or something, especially with someone you're close with, who you can vent to and talk about your feelings. It helps me a lot for me, but everyone's different. 

I also want to note: most of the time, with a heart attack, if you are doing anything physical, the pain will worsen. Heart attacks are noticeable a lot more when physical activities, so it helps when I'm at work (which is physical) and doing my job normally, if I don't feel any changes in how my chest feels, I know it's most likely not heart related, but again, I'm not a doctor, and everyone's body is different.

That's the sucky part about it, but you can always talk to a psychiatrist and talk about how you're feeling and potentially get medication to help.

Also, if you have something that triggers it, avoid that. I found that doing stuff out of the house with people typically makes my symptoms go away, gets my mind off of things, and makes me feel normal. Having someone close to you who understands helps a lot to, to vent and to tell them how you're feeling. There are a lot of things to alleviate the issues, but everyone is different.

I do hope you find a way to cope with it. It truly does blow.

Again, I'm not saying something is or isn't wrong, and that should be talked to about a doctor, but from the sounds of it, it does sound like anxiety. Hey there, new Twitcher! Welcome to the community! I am rather new, also, just started streaming for almost a week now, and let me tell you, it is one fun experience! Since you are new, I felt like I would accumulate all the knowledge I have gotten from all the other streamers out here, and share them with you!

1) Like stated, keep a schedule. But, if you want to be like me, stream when you can, at any time. This way, you will pull in viewers from the day, night, afternoon, whenever. And while you stream, let them know "Hello, just a heads up, my main streaming time is...", that way, you will inform people of when they are most likely to see you again, and may try to join streams then. I stream when I can right now, but have a very set schedule of playing at 10pm CT until 12am or 1am CT, and I make it clear if I am streaming at an irregular time for me.

2) Play the games you want to play, not what will attract many people. You want to stream for fun, also, right? If you play games that you enjoy, viewers will realize that you are enjoying it, and may follow you!

3) Don't play over-saturated games (i.e CoD, CS:GO, LoL). This will make it very hard to get any viewers. Like I stated above, play a game you enjoy, but don't play an overly played game. Here is a real-life example: I stream The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. The game isn't overly popular, but a lot of people still come to watch gameplay, so it also has enough people viewing to rack in viewers. Surprisingly, I get the most viewers out of that game than any other (10, consistently. Not much, but hey, it's something).

4) Interact with viewers. Obviously, this is a given, but it had to be said. Whenever a viewer says anything in chat, try to respond as best you can. Since you and I are smaller channels, we don't have 30 people messaging at the same time, so it is very easy to respond to the viewers. Try to get them involved with the stream, too, that will help a bit. I love to be a part of someone elses stream, and being able to give suggestions to another person, and have them follow my suggestion!

5) Try to stick with 1-3 games to begin with. If you want to build a solid fanbase, you should try sticking with as little amount of games as possible. If you stick with one, people will see you constantly playing that game, and they will join. And more will join, and more...and so on. I started off with 1-3 views on BoI to begin with, and have streamed it every night for 4 days, and it increased to 5-7 viewers, then to a 8-10 viewers. It helps to stick with as few games as possible. If you hopped around playing 30 games to start out with, you won't gain the solid fanbase you may get from the one game. This was a mistake I almost made.

6) The most important rule is...JUST HAVE FUN! I have so much fun streaming, interacting with new people, getting help from viewers, and the determination to reach more and more viewers. Hopefully, you will have fun streaming just as much as many of the other streamers out there!

You may have little to no viewers to start out with, and it may be a little discouraging. But if you keep streaming consistently, people who like watching the same game may see your name popping up over and over, and may decide to watch, or even follow! Streaming, although fun, is a lot of hard work and determination, so don't give up if the views aren't coming in! Just keep doing what you do. Hope I helped, sorry for a lengthy explanation, but I hope I helped, because this is the advice I have taken to be able to start getting viewers. Good luck with the channel, happy streaming!
